points.text: Cartographic skills: atlas and Ordnance Survey maps, maps with photographs.
Graphical skills: construct, choose and interpret graphs, charts and maps.
Numerical and statistical skills: scale, ratio, averages, spread, percentage change and trends.
Use qualitative and quantitative data, including GIS and satellite images.
Build an enquiry and an evidenced argument.
Natural hazards pose major risks to people and property; types and factors affecting risk.
Earthquakes and volcanoes come from processes at plate margins; their global pattern.
Effects of and responses to a tectonic hazard differ between areas of contrasting wealth (two named examples).
Monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce the effects; why people live in hazard zones.

units.title: Weather hazards: global circulation, tropical storms (Cyclone Idai) and UK weather hazards (Somerset floods, 2014)

points.text: Global atmospheric circulation shapes patterns of weather and climate.
Tropical storms form under particular physical conditions; distribution, structure and links to climate change.
Primary and secondary effects of, and responses to, a named tropical storm (school example: Cyclone Idai).
UK weather hazards and a recent extreme event (school example: Somerset Levels floods, 2014).
Evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme.
Evidence for climate change from the Quaternary period to the present.
Natural and human factors causing climate change, and its effects on people and the environment.
Managing climate change: mitigation and adaptation.
Ecosystems involve interaction between biotic and abiotic parts at a range of scales.
A small-scale UK ecosystem: food webs, nutrient cycling and the effect of change.
An overview of the distribution and characteristics of large-scale global ecosystems.

units.title: Tropical rainforests (case study: deforestation in Malaysia)

points.text: Distinctive characteristics of tropical rainforests: climate, soils, plants, animals and biodiversity.
Causes and economic and environmental impacts of deforestation (school case study: Malaysia).
Value of rainforests and strategies for sustainable management.

units.title: Hot deserts (school option; cold environments not taught)

points.text: Distinctive characteristics of hot deserts and how plants and animals adapt.
Opportunities and challenges of developing a hot desert (case study).
Desertification on desert fringes: causes and strategies to reduce it.
The UK's diverse landscapes: location of upland and lowland areas and main river systems.
How geology and past processes created upland and lowland landscapes.

units.title: Coastal landscapes in the UK (examples: Swanage and Lyme Regis)

points.text: Waves, weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition shape the coast.
Erosional and depositional landforms on a named UK coastline (school example: Swanage).
Hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat; a UK coastal management scheme (school example: Lyme Regis).

units.title: River landscapes in the UK (River Tees; flood management at Banbury)

points.text: Long and cross profiles change downstream through erosion, transport and deposition.
Erosional and depositional landforms in a named UK river valley (school example: the River Tees).
Flood risk, hydrographs and hard and soft flood management; a UK scheme (school example: Banbury, taught in Summer).
A synoptic, critical-thinking section on a contemporary issue drawn from 3.1 and 3.2.
Use the pre-release resources booklet issued 12 weeks before the exam.
Weigh stakeholders' views and alternatives; justify a decision.
Two enquiries with primary data in contrasting environments, one physical-human.
Enquiry stages: question, data collection, presentation, analysis, conclusion and evaluation.
Questions on unfamiliar fieldwork materials and on the pupil's own enquiries.

units.title: Urban issues and challenges (case studies: Rio de Janeiro and Bristol)

points.text: Global urbanisation trends, causes and megacities.
Urban growth in an LIC or NEE city (school case study: Rio de Janeiro), with an urban planning example.
Opportunities and challenges in a major UK city (school case study: Bristol), with a regeneration project.
Urban sustainability: resources, green space and transport.

units.title: The changing economic world (case study: Nigeria; the changing UK economy)

points.text: Measuring development, causes of uneven development and the demographic transition model.
Strategies to close the development gap, including a tourism example in an LIC or NEE.
Rapid development in an LIC or NEE (school case study: Nigeria, a newly emerging economy), taught in Spring.
Changes in the UK economy: deindustrialisation, services, regional differences and the UK's place in the world.

units.title: Resource management: food, water and energy in the UK

points.text: Food, water and energy are fundamental to human development; global inequalities.
Changing demand and provision of food, water and energy in the UK.

units.title: Food (school option; water and energy options not taught)

points.text: Global food supply: surplus, deficit and food insecurity.
Strategies to increase food supply, with a large-scale agricultural example and an LIC or NEE local scheme.
Sustainable food supply.
